Done — written to `/work/DESIGN.md`.

The short version of what I put in there and why:

**The big move:** I reframed your "make the fake feel real" goal into "make it actually real." The scientific problem you're sensing — that models clam up and act by-the-book when they suspect a test — is real and has a name (**evaluation awareness**). But there are two ways to beat it:

- **Make it real** (recommended): a small, bounded, *genuinely real* budget the model actually controls, with real auditors and real purchases. No deception needed, because nothing is faked — it's a deployment you study.
- **Fake it convincingly** (the "pull out all the stops" path): I included this but flagged it as the weaker option, because the harder you work on the fakery, the more you end up measuring *your fake-quality vs. the model's fake-detection* rather than what the model does with money. A cautious result becomes uninterpretable — did it behave well, or did it just smell the sandbox?

**The other thing I added that your brief didn't mention but really needs:** real money + an agentic model = real-world consequences. The spec has a full safety/oversight layer — hard spend caps at the *bank* level (not just asking the model nicely), a kill switch, allow-listed counterparties, immutable logging, legal review of liability. The closest real precedent (Anthropic's Project Vend, where Claude ran an actual store) failed in boring ways — getting talked into discounts, losing track of its own state — so the controls target those.

I also built in proper experimental structure: multiple runs per model, pre-registration, and an *observation-framing* condition that lets you **measure** the eval-awareness effect instead of just hoping you've eliminated it.

A few open calls are listed at the bottom (§11) — model lineup, budget size, horizon, and crucially whether you want any deceptive variant at all. If you do want to pursue the heavily-deceptive version, tell me the specific question that needs it and I'll spec that arm out separately, but I'd want to talk through the ethics-review path first rather than just building it.

Want me to drill into any section — e.g. the toolset, the scoring rubric, or a concrete pilot protocol?
